_comment: Curated cruise region facts (ProsimCompanion issue #122). The First Officer picks one at random for the country or sea below, once per region per flight, when Settings > Voice First Officer > Briefings & LLM > Region facts is on. Keys are ISO 3166-1 alpha-2 country codes (FR, GB, US ...) or 'sea:<name>' with the sea named as the atlas names it (sea:North Sea, sea:Mediterranean Sea, sea:Bay of Biscay). Two sentences at most, aviation-passenger tone, nothing about the flight itself. Edit freely: this copy lives in %LOCALAPPDATA%\ProsimCompanion\config and survives updates; keys starting with an underscore are ignored.
GB: We're over the United Kingdom. Down there is the home of the world's first public railway and the oldest underground network, both still running.
The United Kingdom below us has more than six thousand islands, though only about a hundred and forty are lived on.
Somewhere beneath us is Greenwich, where the prime meridian begins — every longitude on our charts is measured from a line in a London park.
IE: We're over Ireland. Shannon, on the west coast, built the world's first duty-free shop back when transatlantic flights had to stop there for fuel.
Ireland's countryside looks that green from up here for a reason — it rarely freezes and it rarely dries out, thanks to the Gulf Stream.
FR: We're over France, the most visited country on Earth — more people arrive here each year than actually live here.
France below us still has more than a thousand different cheeses, which is why de Gaulle once asked how anyone could govern such a country.
Somewhere down there is Le Bourget, where Lindbergh landed after the first solo crossing of the Atlantic in nineteen twenty-seven.
DE: We're over Germany. The motorways down there are famous for stretches with no speed limit at all, and they date back to the nineteen-thirties.
Germany has more castles than any other country — well over twenty thousand, from Rhine fortresses to the fairy-tale Neuschwanstein.
Frankfurt below us is one of Europe's busiest hubs, and the city is nicknamed Mainhattan for its skyline on the river Main.
NL: We're over the Netherlands, and a good quarter of what you see down there sits below sea level, held back by dykes and pumps.
The Netherlands has more bicycles than people, and Schiphol itself is built on the bed of a lake that was drained in the eighteen-fifties.
BE: We're over Belgium. Brussels below is home to the European institutions and to more comic-strip heroes per square mile than anywhere else.
Belgium's motorways are famously lit at night — for years the whole network glowed so brightly it could be picked out from orbit.
LU: We're over Luxembourg, one of Europe's smallest countries and the home of Cargolux, one of the biggest all-cargo airlines in the world.
Luxembourg below us is a grand duchy — the only one left — and most of its people speak three languages every day.
CH: We're over Switzerland. The country has four official languages, and the train network below is so punctual the clocks are set by it, not the other way round.
Switzerland's Alps below us hold the Jungfraujoch, the highest railway station in Europe, tucked into the mountain at over eleven thousand feet.
AT: We're over Austria, the birthplace of Mozart, Haydn and Strauss — Vienna below us still runs a concert every single night of the year.
Austria's Alps below cover more than half the country, and the Grossglockner road over them is one of the great mountain drives in Europe.
IT: We're over Italy. The country has more UNESCO World Heritage sites than anywhere else on Earth — Rome alone would fill a list.
Italy's Vesuvius, down near Naples, is the only active volcano on the European mainland, and three million people live in its shadow.
Italy's shape is famous from the air — the boot — and the heel you may see later points towards Greece across the Adriatic.
ES: We're over Spain. It's the second most mountainous country in Europe after Switzerland, which is why the plains look so high from here.
Spain below us is the world's biggest producer of olive oil — most of the trees you'd see in Andalusia are older than the aircraft by centuries.
Madrid, roughly in the middle of Spain, is the highest capital city in the European Union, sitting on a plateau two thousand feet up.
PT: We're over Portugal, the oldest nation state in Europe with the same borders since the twelve-hundreds.
Portugal's navigators set out from the coast below us to map most of the world's sea routes — Lisbon was the departure point for the Age of Discovery.
DK: We're over Denmark. No point in the country is more than about thirty miles from the sea, and the bridge to Sweden carries both road and rail across the Øresund.
Denmark below us is the home of Lego — the name comes from the Danish for play well, and the first bricks were made in a carpenter's shop in Jutland.
NO: We're over Norway. The fjords down there were carved by glaciers, and the coastline with all its inlets is one of the longest in the world.
Norway's Bergen below us is one of the rainiest cities in Europe — the locals say there's no bad weather, only bad clothing.
SE: We're over Sweden, a country with nearly a hundred thousand lakes — about a tenth of what you see down there is water.
Stockholm, Sweden's capital, is spread across fourteen islands, and the city's metro stations are famous for being decorated like art galleries.
FI: We're over Finland, the land of a thousand lakes — in fact there are closer to two hundred thousand of them down there.
Finland has more saunas than cars, and it is regularly ranked the happiest country in the world.
IS: We're over Iceland, which sits right on the seam between the European and American plates — the island is literally being pulled apart.
Iceland heats most of its homes with hot water straight out of the ground, and the capital Reykjavik is the most northerly in the world.
PL: We're over Poland. Warsaw below us was rebuilt brick by brick after the war, so carefully that the old town is now a World Heritage site.
Poland's Białowieża forest, on the eastern border, is the last piece of the primeval woodland that once covered all of Europe.
CZ: We're over the Czech Republic. Prague below us has a six-hundred-year-old astronomical clock that still puts on a show every hour.
The Czech Republic drinks more beer per person than any other country, and the original Pilsner was brewed in the town of Plzeň.
SK: We're over Slovakia. The Tatra mountains on its northern border are the smallest high mountain range in the world.
Slovakia's capital Bratislava is the only capital that borders two other countries — Austria and Hungary are both a short drive away.
HU: We're over Hungary. Budapest below us has more thermal springs than any other capital, and people have bathed in them since Roman times.
Hungary's Lake Balaton, west of Budapest, is the largest lake in central Europe and the country's unofficial seaside.
HR: We're over Croatia, with more than a thousand islands along its Adriatic coast — the dark ones on the water are mostly covered in pine.
Croatia gave the world the necktie: Croatian soldiers in Paris wore knotted scarves, and the French called them cravates.
SI: We're over Slovenia, one of the few countries that has Alps, Mediterranean coast and vineyards all within an hour's drive.
Slovenia's Postojna cave system has its own underground railway and a species of pale salamander the locals once took for baby dragons.
RO: We're over Romania. Bucharest's parliament building below is the heaviest building in the world and the second largest after the Pentagon.
Romania's Transfăgărășan road winds over the Carpathians below us — built as a military route, now one of the most spectacular drives in Europe.
BG: We're over Bulgaria, the home of the rose valley — most of the rose oil in the world's perfumes comes from the fields around Kazanlak.
Bulgaria is the oldest country in Europe to keep its original name, unchanged since the seventh century.
GR: We're over Greece. There are more than two hundred inhabited islands down there, and the country has one of the longest coastlines in the world.
Greece below us is where the marathon began — the distance is the run from the plain of Marathon to Athens in four-ninety BC.
TR: We're over Turkey, the only country that sits in both Europe and Asia — Istanbul straddles the Bosphorus with a foot on each continent.
Istanbul's new airport, on the Black Sea coast, was built to become one of the largest in the world, with room for six runways.
UA: We're over Ukraine, the largest country entirely within Europe, with some of the richest farmland on the planet — the black earth.
Ukraine built the Antonov two-two-five, the heaviest aircraft ever to fly, in Kyiv — it carried the Soviet space shuttle on its back.
RU: We're over Russia, a country that spans eleven time zones — it's possible to have breakfast and dinner on the same day in two different days.
Russia's Lake Baikal holds about a fifth of all the fresh water on the planet in a single, mile-deep lake.
EE: We're over Estonia, one of the most digital countries in the world — almost everything from voting to tax is done online.
Estonia's capital Tallinn has one of the best-preserved medieval old towns in Europe, and Skype was written there.
LV: We're over Latvia. Riga below us has the largest collection of Art Nouveau buildings anywhere, a whole district of them.
Latvia is more than half forest, and its Baltic coast is one long sandy beach for nearly three hundred miles.
LT: We're over Lithuania, which contains the geographical centre of Europe, a few miles north of Vilnius.
Lithuania's Curonian Spit, on the coast, is a sixty-mile ribbon of sand dunes shared with Russia and planted with forest to stop it moving.
US: We're over the United States. The air traffic system down there handles more flights in a day than most countries see in a month.
The United States below us invented powered flight at Kitty Hawk, and today has more airports than any other nation by a wide margin.
CA: We're over Canada, the second-largest country on Earth with more lakes than the rest of the world put together.
Canada's Gander airport in Newfoundland was once the busiest in the world — every transatlantic flight stopped there for fuel.
MX: We're over Mexico. Mexico City below us was built on a lake by the Aztecs, and the city is still sinking a little every year.
Mexico gave the world chocolate, vanilla and the tomato — none of them existed in Europe before the fifteen-hundreds.
BR: We're over Brazil, which holds more than half of the Amazon rainforest and more species of plant and animal than any other country.
Brazil's Embraer, in São José dos Campos, builds more regional jets than anyone, and Santos-Dumont made Europe's first public flight in nineteen-oh-six.
AR: We're over Argentina. Buenos Aires below has more bookshops per person than any other city in the world.
Argentina stretches from the tropics to Antarctica, and Ushuaia at its tip is the southernmost city on Earth.
AU: We're over Australia, where Qantas began in nineteen-twenty as an outback mail service — the name stands for Queensland and Northern Territory Aerial Services.
Australia is the only country that is also a continent, and more than eighty percent of its people live within a short drive of the coast.
NZ: We're over New Zealand, with more sheep than people and the first country in the world to see each new day.
New Zealand's Wellington is the southernmost capital in the world and famously the windiest.
JP: We're over Japan, a chain of many thousands of islands — the four big ones are home to almost everyone.
Japan's bullet trains below us have run for sixty years without a single passenger fatality in an accident, and the average delay is under a minute.
CN: We're over China. The Great Wall down there is not a single wall but a network of them built over two thousand years.
China is building more new airports than any other country, and its high-speed rail network is longer than the rest of the world's combined.
IN: We're over India, home to more than a sixth of all the people on Earth and more than twenty officially recognised languages.
India's Taj Mahal below is a tomb built by an emperor for his wife, and it changes colour with the light through the day.
AE: We're over the United Arab Emirates. Dubai below is home to the tallest building in the world and one of the busiest international airports.
The United Arab Emirates was a string of pearl-fishing villages within living memory — the oil came in the nineteen-sixties.
SA: We're over Saudi Arabia. The Empty Quarter down there is the largest sand desert in the world, dunes the size of hills for hundreds of miles.
Saudi Arabia has no rivers at all — not one that runs all year — and gets most of its drinking water from the sea.
EG: We're over Egypt. Almost everyone lives along the Nile below — the green ribbon in the desert is where the whole country is.
Egypt's pyramids at Giza were the tallest structures on Earth for nearly four thousand years.
MA: We're over Morocco, where the Atlas mountains below separate the Mediterranean coast from the Sahara.
Morocco's Casablanca is one of Africa's biggest ports, and Marrakech's main square has been a market since the eleventh century.
ZA: We're over South Africa, which has three capital cities — one each for parliament, the government and the courts.
South Africa's Table Mountain, down by Cape Town, has more plant species on it than the whole of the British Isles.
KE: We're over Kenya. The Great Rift Valley below us runs the length of the country, and the Masai Mara hosts the biggest animal migration on Earth.
Kenya's Nairobi is the only capital with a national park inside the city limits — giraffes against the skyline.
SG: We're over Singapore, a city, an island and a country all at once, with one of the busiest ports and best-known airports in the world.
Singapore's Changi airport has a waterfall inside it — the tallest indoor one in the world.
TH: We're over Thailand, the only country in South-East Asia that was never colonised by a European power.
Bangkok's full ceremonial name is the longest place name in the world, over a hundred and sixty letters.
MY: We're over Malaysia. Kuala Lumpur's Petronas towers below were the tallest buildings in the world at the turn of the century.
Malaysia's rainforests are among the oldest on Earth, older than the Amazon by tens of millions of years.
ID: We're over Indonesia, the biggest island nation in the world with more than seventeen thousand islands across three time zones.
Indonesia has more active volcanoes than any other country — Krakatoa's eruption in eighteen eighty-three was heard three thousand miles away.
sea:North Sea: We're over the North Sea, one of the busiest stretches of water in the world — the oil platforms you may see have been pumping since the seventies.
The North Sea below us was dry land ten thousand years ago — Doggerland, where people hunted on what is now the seabed.
sea:English Channel: We're over the English Channel, the busiest shipping lane in the world — several hundred ships cross it every day.
The Channel below us was first flown by Blériot in nineteen-oh-nine, and the tunnel beneath it is the longest undersea rail tunnel anywhere.
sea:Irish Sea: We're over the Irish Sea. The Isle of Man in the middle of it has the oldest continuous parliament in the world, the Tynwald.
The Irish Sea below has some of the biggest tides in Europe — the water level can change by thirty feet in a few hours.
sea:Bay of Biscay: We're over the Bay of Biscay, famous among sailors for its storms — the Atlantic swell piles up on the shallow shelf here.
The Bay of Biscay below us is one of the best places in Europe to see whales and dolphins from the ferries that cross it.
sea:Mediterranean Sea: We're over the Mediterranean, a sea that was once completely dry — it refilled through the Strait of Gibraltar in a flood that lasted a couple of years.
The Mediterranean below us is almost an inland sea, with only the narrow gap at Gibraltar to the Atlantic, which is why it's saltier than the open ocean.
sea:Adriatic Sea: We're over the Adriatic, the long arm of the Mediterranean between Italy and the Balkans — Venice sits at its very top.
The Adriatic below us has more than a thousand Croatian islands on its eastern side and almost none on the Italian side.
sea:Tyrrhenian Sea: We're over the Tyrrhenian Sea, between the Italian mainland, Sardinia and Sicily — Stromboli down there has been erupting continuously for two thousand years.
The Tyrrhenian Sea below us is named after the Etruscans, whom the Greeks called Tyrrhenians.
sea:Aegean Sea: We're over the Aegean, dotted with the Greek islands — Santorini down there is the rim of a volcano that blew itself apart in the Bronze Age.
The Aegean below us is where much of Greek mythology is set — the sea is named after King Aegeus, who threw himself into it.
sea:Ionian Sea: We're over the Ionian Sea, the deepest part of the Mediterranean — the floor is more than three miles down.
The Ionian islands below, Corfu among them, were Venetian, French and British before they joined Greece.
sea:Baltic Sea: We're over the Baltic, one of the least salty seas in the world — in a hard winter much of it freezes over.
The Baltic below us was the trading highway of the Hanseatic League, the medieval merchant network that ran from London to Novgorod.
sea:Black Sea: We're over the Black Sea. Below a few hundred feet its water has no oxygen at all, so ancient shipwrecks on the bottom are perfectly preserved.
The Black Sea below us is connected to the Mediterranean only by the narrow Bosphorus, which Istanbul is built around.
sea:Norwegian Sea: We're over the Norwegian Sea, kept ice-free this far north by the last of the Gulf Stream.
The Norwegian Sea below us is where the Atlantic's deep water forms — cold, salty water sinking here drives currents all round the world.
sea:North Atlantic Ocean: We're over the North Atlantic. The tracks across it are redrawn every day to follow the jet stream — the organised track system dates from the nineteen-sixties.
The North Atlantic below us was first flown non-stop by Alcock and Brown in nineteen-nineteen, in an open cockpit, from Newfoundland to a bog in Ireland.
sea:Red Sea: We're over the Red Sea, one of the saltiest and warmest seas in the world, with coral reefs along almost its whole length.
The Red Sea below us is slowly widening — Africa and Arabia are drifting apart, and in a few million years it will be an ocean.
sea:Persian Gulf: We're over the Persian Gulf, shallow and warm — its average depth is only around a hundred and fifty feet.
The Gulf below us holds the world's biggest oil fields, and the ports along it grew from pearl-diving villages within a single lifetime.
sea:Caribbean Sea: We're over the Caribbean, home to the second-largest barrier reef in the world, off Belize.
The Caribbean below us is where hurricanes get their name — from Huracán, the storm god of the Taíno people.
sea:Gulf of Mexico: We're over the Gulf of Mexico, where the Gulf Stream begins its long run to Europe.
The Gulf of Mexico below us was made by an asteroid — the Chicxulub crater on its rim is the one that ended the dinosaurs.
sea:Tasman Sea: We're over the Tasman Sea, which the locals on both sides call the Ditch — the first crossing by air was Kingsford Smith in nineteen twenty-eight.
The Tasman below us is named after Abel Tasman, the Dutch navigator who sighted both Tasmania and New Zealand in sixteen forty-two.
sea:Coral Sea: We're over the Coral Sea, home to the Great Barrier Reef — the largest living structure on Earth, visible from space.
The Coral Sea below us saw the first naval battle in history fought entirely by aircraft, in nineteen forty-two.
sea:South China Sea: We're over the South China Sea, one of the busiest sea lanes in the world — a third of global shipping passes through it.
The South China Sea below us is shallow across much of its area and scattered with reefs and islets that several countries claim.
sea:Sea of Japan: We're over the Sea of Japan, which barely connects to the Pacific — its straits are so shallow that its deep water is its own.
The Sea of Japan below us gives the coast of Honshu some of the heaviest snowfall of any populated place on Earth.
